rounds.hypothesis: Exactly as diagnosed: sys_set_priority has no ownership/credential check at all, so an unprivileged caller targeting pid 1 falls straight through to the RLIMIT_NICE arm and the first error it can produce is EACCES. The fix is not to reorder anything -- the EPERM half does not exist -- but to add the missing authorisation predicate at the credential layer and call it per target process, above the RLIMIT_NICE arm, so EPERM strictly precedes EACCES.
rounds.change: Added kernel/src/process/priority.rs with `check_set_priority_perm(target_process, ctx)`, modelled on the two existing sibling predicates check_signal_perm (process/kill.rs:161) and check_rlimit_perm (syscall/prlimit64.rs:97): it returns Ok when the caller's euid equals the target main thread's ruid or euid, else when lsm_hooks::on_capable(CapableContext::new(target_process.user_ns().lock().as_ref(), ctx.posix_thread, CapSet::SYS_NICE)) succeeds, else EPERM. Exported it from process/mod.rs and called it as the first statement inside the `for process in processes.iter()` loop in sys_set_priority, above the RLIMIT_NICE lookup. Nothing else was touched -- the nice clamp, the RLIMIT_NICE comparison and the FIXME about fair-scheduler thread state are unchanged.
rounds.outcome: green on the first round. Selector run: `setpriority02: pass (0.001s)` at qemu.log:43, TEST SUMMARY Passed: 7 / Failed: 0 / Broken: 0 / Skipped: 0 / Warnings: 0, `All conformance tests passed.`, make exit 0. Baseline was 6 pass / 1 fail. `cargo check` and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` on aster-kernel are clean and `tools/format_all.sh --check` is silent.

layer: The process-credential permission layer, matching diagnose.json's owning_layer exactly. The predicate lives in kernel/src/process/priority.rs, beside kill.rs's check_signal_perm and reachable by any future priority-setting syscall, rather than inline in the syscall body. That is Linux's placement too: set_one_prio_perm sits in kernel/sys.c, above set_user_nice() in kernel/sched/core.c, precisely so every entry point that changes another task's priority shares one rule. Nothing in kernel/src/sched/ was touched, and the syscall file gained only a call plus a comment.
generalizes:
The predicate branches on nothing the test supplies. It reads only the caller's euid, the target's ruid/euid and CAP_SYS_NICE, and it is applied per target process inside the get_processes loop -- so it is correct for the two fan-out arms setpriority02 never exercises in the multi-member case: PRIO_PGRP over a group whose members have differing credentials, and PRIO_USER over every process of a uid. Placing it once at the syscall entry against `who` would have been the overfitted shape, since it would silently authorise every other member of the group; the loop placement refuses each unauthorised member on its own credentials. Two behaviours exist only for inputs this test cannot produce: the CAP_SYS_NICE bypass (root never lowers another process's nice in setpriority02, so the capability arm is never taken during the run) and the target-euid comparison (the test's targets are pid 1, whose ruid and euid are both 0, so only the ruid arm is load-bearing there -- the euid arm matters for a setuid target, which the test has none of).

The cases that an over-eager fix would have broken are pinned by the test itself and stayed green: subtests 5 and 6 must remain EACCES rather than becoming EPERM, and they do, because the target is the caller's own process (and its own group), so euid == ruid and the predicate falls through to the RLIMIT_NICE arm untouched. Subtests 1-4 stay EINVAL/ESRCH because PriorityTarget::new and get_processes both run before the loop is entered.

Other callers: sys_get_priority is a read and needs no check; Asterinas implements no sys_nice (syscall 34 is sys_pause in the x86 table), which is Linux's other route into set_one_prio. So sys_set_priority is the only caller today and the only one this patch changes. The value of the credential-layer placement is that the same gap in sys_sched_setattr / sys_sched_setscheduler / sys_sched_setparam (all via access_sched_attr_with in syscall/sched_getattr.rs:197) and in sys_ioprio_set is now fixable by calling this predicate, with no rule to re-derive. Those remain unfixed and out of scope, as diagnose.json specified.

Regression sweep beyond the target, one boot, 13 tests across the whole priority/nice/sched-priority surface: getpriority01, getpriority02, nice02, nice03, ioprio_get01, ioprio_set02, sched_setparam01, sched_setscheduler04, sched_get_priority_max01, sched_get_priority_min01 and setpriority02 all pass -- 43 passed / 0 failed / 0 broken. nice02 and nice03 matter most: glibc's nice() routes through setpriority when SYS_nice is absent, so they exercise the patched path as an unprivileged caller against its own process and confirm the self-targeting fast path is not broken. The two skips (ioprio_set01, sched_setparam03) are both in the pre-existing skip set recorded by earlier runs, not new.
fix_summary:
Adds the authorisation half of Linux's set_one_prio pair, which Asterinas was missing entirely: before a process's nice value may be altered on behalf of a caller, the caller must own the target (euid equal to the target's real or effective uid) or hold CAP_SYS_NICE in the target's user namespace, and that refusal is EPERM decided strictly before any RLIMIT_NICE check on the requested value.

The abstraction chosen is a free function in the process-credential layer taking (&Process, &Context), which is the shape Asterinas already uses twice for exactly this kind of caller-vs-target question -- check_signal_perm and check_rlimit_perm -- rather than a method on Credentials or a Linux-style task-struct predicate. Two Asterinas-specific consequences follow. First, the target's credentials are read from its main thread via Process::main_thread().as_posix_thread(), because Asterinas keeps credentials per PosixThread while nice is a per-Process attribute (process/mod.rs:114-117 says as much); the main thread is the process's representative credential set, which is the same resolution check_rlimit_perm makes. Second, the capability check goes through lsm_hooks::on_capable with a CapableContext rather than reading effective_capset() directly, so the check passes through the LSM stack like every other capability decision in the tree and inherits the user-namespace FIXME already documented in modules/capability.rs instead of adding a second one.

CapSet::SYS_NICE already existed at credentials/capabilities.rs:34 and was referenced nowhere; this is its first use.

One deliberate non-change, worth flagging for review: Linux's setpriority loop keeps going after a per-target error (`error = set_one_prio(p, niceval, error)`) and so still applies the new nice to the other group members, whereas Asterinas returns early. That early return is pre-existing -- the RLIMIT_NICE arm already did it -- and the new check follows the same shape rather than changing loop semantics, which the invariant does not require and which would be a larger change than this fix warrants.
